<reflection>
The baseline experiment with [S]=1.0, [cat]=0.01, [P]=0.0 produced fitting results where most mechanisms (M1, M2, M6-M20 except M4, M5) give nearly identical NLL values (~-20.2). Only M4 and M5 are clearly rejected. This suggests the baseline kinetics are well-described by simple Michaelis-Menten-like behavior, and all the "extended" mechanisms collapse to this baseline when their extra pathway (dimerization, deactivation, inhibition) isn't strongly activated. My aim to discriminate broadly was not achieved - I need to design experiments that perturb specific mechanistic features.
</reflection>

<hypothesis>
To distinguish among the remaining mechanisms, I need to activate the "extra" pathways that differentiate them from M1 (basic Michaelis-Menten). Key distinguishing features:
- **High [cat]**: amplifies cat-dimerization (M2, M3, M13) and cat-cat deactivation (M13, M19). Also tests catalyst-order dependence.
- **High [P] initial**: tests product inhibition (M12, M17) and reversibility.
- **High [S]**: tests substrate inhibition (M7, M11, M16) and saturation.
- **Added product early**: tests M12, M17.

A high catalyst loading experiment is maximally informative because:
1. It tests whether rate scales linearly with [cat] (M1) or sub-linearly (M2, M3, M13, M19 - dimerization/bimolecular deactivation).
2. Deactivation mechanisms with cat²-order (M13, M19) will show more pronounced effects at high [cat].
3. M6 (catalyst activation) and M8 (equilibrium cat↔cat*) would behave differently at high [cat] vs low [cat].
4. Time-dependent deactivation (M9, M14, M20) will show curvature.

I'll use moderate substrate and significantly higher catalyst loading.
</hypothesis>
